Dina Ercilia Boluarte Zegarra (born 31 May 1962) is a Peruvian politician, civil servant, and lawyer who served as the president of Peru from 7 December 2022 until she was removed from office on 10 October 2025. She had previously served as the first vice president and minister at the Ministry of Development and Social Inclusion under President Pedro Castillo. She served as an officer at the National Registry of Identification and Civil Status (RENIEC) from 2007 until 2022. Boluarte is the first woman to become President of Peru.
As such, she was labeled "the world's least popular leader" and the "most unpopular leader in the world". On 10 October 2025, Boluarte was impeached and removed from office by the Peruvian Congress in a 122–0 vote amidst a security crisis and renewed civil unrest against her rule. She was succeeded as President of Peru by José Jerí, the president of Congress.
Bolivia, Colombia, Honduras, Mexico and Venezuela supported Pedro Castillo as the President of Peru following the events in December 2022 and refused to recognize Boluarte. The issue of international recognition soon after became irrelevant as she received recognition as the legitimate president from most international leaders.
The mainstream press, which is mostly opposed to Castillo's government, supported Boluarte's administration, which moved away from the left and aligned itself with conservative parties, seeking to protect markets and preserve the economic model which has been the status quo in the country for the past two decades. ↑ Noriega, Carlos (20 December 2022). results.name: Peru's First Female President: Keiko Fujimori's Historic Mandate - Amazons Watch Magazine
results.content:
*“The rise of women to the highest offices of government is not merely a political achievement; it is a testament to the progress of democracy and the limitless potential of women’s leadership.”*  
History was made on 28 July 2026 when Keiko Sofía Fujimori Higuchi shattered one of Peru’s most enduring political barriers by becoming the country’s first woman elected president through a democratic popular vote. Her inauguration on Peru’s Independence Day marked not only a personal triumph after three unsuccessful presidential bids but also a defining moment for women’s political leadership in Latin America.  
Assuming office during one of the most challenging periods in Peru’s recent history, Fujimori inherited a nation grappling with political instability, economic uncertainty, rising insecurity, and declining public confidence in government. As Peru’s 10th president in just over a decade, she now shoulders the responsibility of restoring stability, strengthening democratic institutions, revitalising the economy, and rebuilding trust among Peruvians.
Her pursuit of the presidency was marked by extraordinary persistence. She contested four presidential elections, narrowly losing the run-off in 2011 to Ollanta Humala, in 2016 to Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, and in 2021 to Pedro Castillo. Despite these setbacks, she remained a dominant force in Peruvian politics, continuously rebuilding her political base and maintaining her position as the country’s leading opposition figure.  
Her perseverance finally paid off during the 2026 presidential election, when she defeated left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez in one of the closest elections in Peru’s democratic history. Fujimori secured approximately 50.1 percent of the vote, prevailing by fewer than 50,000 votes out of more than 18 million ballots cast. The victory secured her place in history as Peru’s first woman elected president through a democratic popular vote.  
**Leading Peru through Uncertain Times**  
Keiko Fujimori was inaugurated on 28 July 2026, coinciding with Peru’s 205th Independence Day celebrations. She assumed office at a time when the country faced political polarisation, economic challenges, institutional instability, and growing concerns over crime and public safety.
Recognizing these pressing national issues, her administration outlined an ambitious agenda focused on restoring security, strengthening democratic governance, encouraging private investment, stimulating economic growth, expanding employment opportunities, and improving essential public services. Her government has also prioritized combating organised crime, enhancing internal security, and implementing social programmes aimed at improving the quality of life for Peru’s citizens.  
In her inaugural address, President Fujimori called on Peruvians to move beyond years of political division and work together toward national renewal. She pledged to rebuild confidence in public institutions, foster inclusive economic development, and create a more stable and prosperous future for generations to come.  
**A Historic Presidency**  
Keiko Fujimori’s election represents more than a personal political achievement; it marks a historic milestone for women’s leadership in Peru and across Latin America. By becoming the first woman democratically elected to lead the Republic of Peru, she has broken one of the nation’s highest political glass ceilings and demonstrated that perseverance, experience, and public service can redefine the boundaries of leadership.

results.name: Keiko Fujimori wins Peru presidency in tight race
results.content:
## Keiko Fujimori secured Peru's presidency by a margin of 49,641 votes following the completion of ballot counting, becoming the first woman elected to lead the Andean nation and capping a political comeback after three previous defeats, more than 500 days in pretrial detention, and a campaign plagued by the shadow of her father's imprisonment.  
Keiko Fujimori has claimed Peru’s presidency following a historically narrow victory over Roberto Sanchez, with the National Office of Electoral Processes confirming a final margin of 49,641 votes after completing its ballot review Monday and cementing her position as the first woman elected to lead the Andean nation.
## Narrowest Margin in Modern History  
The official declaration concluded weeks of meticulous scrutiny of contested ballots across the 92,766 electoral minutes cast in the race. Fujimori, running under the conservative Fuerza Popular banner, edged out the Juntos por el Peru coalition candidate to secure the 2026-2031 constitutional term. The result marks the culmination of one of Peru’s most fiercely contested presidential races in recent memory, settling a contest that remained deadlocked throughout the counting process and delivering a mandate that rests on less than half a percentage point of the national vote.
## Family Legacy and Incoming Administration  
Fujimori’s political identity remains intertwined with the complex legacy of her father, former President Alberto Fujimori, who is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence for corruption and crimes against humanity. She entered public life in 1994 at age 19 as first lady following her parents' separation, later founding Fuerza Popular in 2009 to carve her own path within Peru’s conservative political landscape.  
Peruvian law dictates she will take office July 28 alongside First Vice President Luis Galarreta Velarde, a former Congress president, and Second Vice President Miguel Angel Torres Morales, a constitutional attorney. The incoming administration faces immediate pressure to consolidate support in a deeply divided legislature while managing the ongoing shadow of her father's imprisonment and the judicial proceedings that have shadowed her own career.

results.name: Keiko Fujimori wins the presidency in Peru
results.content:
**Related videos:**  
**Keiko Fujimori** became the elected president of Peru on Monday after the completion of 100% of the tally of ballots from the presidential runoff, according to the [official results](https://resultadosegundavuelta.onpe.gob.pe/main/resumen) published by the ONPE, the National Office of Electoral Processes.  
The candidate from **Fuerza Popular** received **50.135%** of the valid votes, equivalent to 9,223,396 ballots, compared to 49.865% and 9,173,755 votes for the leftist Roberto Sánchez Palomino, from Juntos por el Perú.  
The difference between the two was just **49,641 votes**, one of the narrowest margins recorded in a Peruvian presidential election in recent decades, according to *BBC*.  
The runoff took place on June 7 in a climate of strong political polarization, and the processing of disputed and challenged ballots extended the counting period for 22 days, during which Sánchez gained a lead only to lose it in the final stretch.  
A decisive factor was the vote from abroad: Fujimori dominated with 63.4% of the ballots cast outside of Peru—184,435 votes compared to 106,338 for his rival—with support of 76.5% among Peruvians living in the United States.  
Sánchez's party filed a lawsuit to annul the votes from abroad, claiming irregularities, but the **National Jury of Elections (JNE)** had already dismissed previous requests for being submitted beyond the legal deadline.
The president of the JNE, Roberto Burneo, denied any narrative of fraud and confirmed that the election took place with "full normalcy and regularity."  
The result still needs to be formally announced by the JNE, the body responsible for resolving the final challenges and officially declaring the elected president for the 2026-2031 term.  
If the process goes smoothly, Fujimori would take office on **July 28**.  
After the conclusion of the counting, Fujimori herself reacted on the social network X: "We await the proclamation from the JNE with great humility, prudence, and responsibility. We are increasingly closer to starting a path of order and hope for all Peruvians."  
At 51 years old, Fujimori becomes the **first woman elected president of Peru through popular vote**, as the former president Dina Boluarte took office in 2022 through constitutional succession following the dismissal of Pedro Castillo, not through direct election.  
This victory comes in her fourth consecutive attempt for the presidency, after losing the run-offs in 2011 to Ollanta Humala, in 2016 to Pedro Pablo Kuczynski by just 42,000 votes, and in 2021 to Pedro Castillo.  
Fujimori will also be the ninth person to hold the presidency of Peru in the last ten years, a country marked by a [deep political instability](https://www.bbc.com/mundo/articles/cjwg1xdjvyjo) in which most of its leaders left office amid accusations of corruption or parliamentary procedures to remove them.
His father, former president Alberto Fujimori, who governed Peru from 1990 to 2000, [passed away on September 12, 2024](https://en.cibercuba.com/noticias/2024-09-12-u1-e135253-s27061-nid288299-muere-expresidente-peruano-alberto-fujimori) at the age of 86 without seeing his daughter come to power.  
With the consolidated results and the JNE's proclamation as the only pending step, Fujimori inherits a highly polarized country and faces the challenge of achieving the stability that eluded all of his recent predecessors.

results.content:
**Getting your**  
[Trinity Audio](https://trinityaudio.ai)player ready...  
Keiko Fujimori was sworn in as Peru’s president on Tuesday, becoming the first woman ever elected by popular vote to lead the country. Her inauguration marks the return of Fujimorismo to power 26 years after the collapse of the authoritarian regime led by her father, Alberto Fujimori, and opens a new chapter for a nation that has spent the past decade plagued by political instability and a constant turnover of presidents.  
The Popular Force leader took office after one of the closest presidential elections in Peru’s recent history. Fujimori defeated left-wing candidate [Roberto Sanchez](https://colombiaone.com/2026/06/23/peru-roberto-sanchez-wont-recognize-keiko-fujimori-president/) by just 49,641 votes, a margin of slightly more than two-tenths of a percentage point. The razor-thin result triggered legal challenges, court appeals, and fraud allegations from the defeated camp before Peru’s National Jury of Elections officially certified the outcome.  
The presidential inauguration, following the elections, takes place on July 28 under a constitutional mandate, coinciding with the anniversary of the country’s Proclamation of Independence, declared by Jose de San Martín in 1821. The date is a centerpiece of Peru’s Independence Day celebrations and was adopted through political and historical tradition to symbolize the beginning of each new presidential term.
## Keiko Fujimori sworn In as Peru’s first elected female president  
Although [Dina Boluarte](https://colombiaone.com/2025/10/10/peru-removes-president-dina-boluarte-jose-jeri/) was the first woman to serve as Peru’s president, she assumed office through constitutional succession following the impeachment of Pedro Castillo in December 2022. [Keiko Fujimori](https://x.com/KeikoFujimori?lang=en), by contrast, became the first woman to win the country’s highest office through a popular vote—an achievement widely regarded as historic in a nation where no female candidate had prevailed at the ballot box in more than two centuries of republican history.  
The victory also capped Fujimori’s long electoral journey. After losing three presidential elections and enduring years of judicial investigations and intense political polarization, the conservative leader finally reached the presidency at the helm of a movement that continues to inspire both strong support and fierce opposition.
Her last name remains one of the most controversial in Peruvian politics. To her supporters, [Alberto Fujimori](https://colombiaone.com/2024/09/12/alberto-fujimori-peru-died/) was the president who defeated the Shining Path insurgency and stabilized the economy during the 1990s. However, his administration was also marked by serious human rights violations, corruption, authoritarianism, and a lengthy prison sentence for crimes against humanity. That legacy will inevitably shadow the new president’s administration.  
Fujimori enters office facing the immediate challenge of governing a deeply polarized country. The narrow election result exposed a society almost evenly divided, with a large segment of the population continuing to question the political legitimacy of her government, even after electoral authorities rejected all legal challenges and officially declared her the winner.  
Public security ranks among her most pressing priorities. During the campaign, she pledged to intensify the fight against organized crime, crack down on extortion, and strengthen the state’s presence in response to rising violence affecting multiple regions of the country. She must also revive the economy, encourage private investment, and address the aftermath of recent natural disasters that have struck several parts of Peru.

results.name: Peru Presidential election 2026 — Results | ElectioMap
results.content:
About this election  
Peru held its presidential election in two rounds: a first round on 12 April 2026 (held alongside the congressional elections) and a run-off on 7 June 2026. With 100% of tally sheets (actas) processed — all 92,766 of them — Keiko Fujimori of Fuerza Popular defeated Roberto Sánchez of Juntos por el Perú by 50.135% to 49.865%, a margin of 49,641 votes out of 18,397,151 valid ballots. Sánchez had led throughout most of the count before Fujimori edged ahead in the final stretch, as tally sheets from Lima, the north coast and the diaspora were processed. **The result is official and final: on 3 July 2026 the National Elections Jury (JNE) formally proclaimed Keiko Fujimori president-elect for the 2026–2031 term**, together with her elected vice-presidents Luis Galarreta and Miguel Ángel Torres. She becomes the first woman elected president of Peru, and takes office on 28 July 2026. The department-by-department map below shows the official ONPE count: Fujimori carried Lima, Callao and the northern coastal departments, while Sánchez swept the southern Andes.
Peru elects its president by two-round majority vote: if no candidate exceeds 50% of valid votes in the first round, the top two advance to a run-off. The president serves a five-year term and may not be re-elected to consecutive terms. Elections are administered by the ONPE, while the JNE resolves disputes and proclaims the official final result. Voting is compulsory.  
Peru has experienced chronic instability, cycling through six presidents in the decade before 2026 amid repeated impeachments, resignations and confrontation between the executive and Congress. The election was held under the caretaker presidency that followed the removal of Pedro Castillo in December 2022 and the troubled, deeply unpopular tenure of his successor Dina Boluarte, whose government faced mass protests and a sharp loss of public confidence.  
The presidential first round was held on the same day as elections to a newly restored bicameral Congress, in which Keiko Fujimori's Fuerza Popular emerged as the largest party in both chambers without a majority. Whoever wins the presidency will therefore face a fragmented legislature — and, given Peru's recent history of executive-legislative warfare, the composition of Congress is at least as important as the presidency for the country's stability.
With the JNE proclamation of 3 July 2026, the result is final. Fujimori and her vice-presidents receive their credentials on 15 July, and the inauguration takes place on 28 July 2026 — Peru's independence day — for the 2026–2031 term, succeeding interim president José María Balcázar. Fujimori will govern alongside the new bicameral Congress elected in April, in which her Fuerza Popular is the largest party in both chambers but holds no majority, so her administration will still depend on coalition-building. After three failed run-offs, the first woman to win Peru's presidency inherits a polarised country: nearly half the electorate voted against her, her opponent disputes her legitimacy, and the southern Andes — where Sánchez won by margins above 70% — remain the heartland of the opposition.  
The contest is inseparable from the Fujimori name. Keiko's father, Alberto Fujimori, who governed Peru in the 1990s, remains one of the most polarising figures in the country's history — credited by supporters with defeating the Shining Path insurgency and taming hyperinflation, but later convicted of human-rights abuses and corruption. Keiko has built Fuerza Popular into Peru's most disciplined political organisation while herself facing protracted corruption proceedings. For many Peruvians a Fujimori run-off is, once again, as much a referendum for or against *fujimorismo* as a straightforward choice between left and right.

results.name: Keiko Fujimori returns family dynasty to power in Peru after 30 years - UPI.com
results.content:
After 15 years of failed attempts and four presidential campaigns, Keiko Fujimori became Peru's first woman elected president by popular vote
July 28 (UPI) -- After 15 years of failed attempts and four presidential campaigns, Keiko Fujimori on Tuesday became Peru's first woman elected president by popular vote, returning her family's political movement to the Government Palace after nearly three decades.
Fujimori, the daughter and political heir of former Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, took office on the same date her father did in 1990. She assumes leadership of a country that faces a severe public security crisis and the immediate challenge of governing a fractured nation. Her inauguration also marks the return to power of the Fujimori political movement, which remains deeply divisive in Peru.
Although the tough-on-crime platform helped her win the presidency, it also raised concerns among political opponents and human rights advocates. They warn that her policies could repeat abuses for which Alberto Fujimori was convicted. Fujimori also will have to build political agreements after years of instability that have left Peru with eight presidents in 10 years.
The governing bloc holds more than one-third of the votes, enough to block attempts by the leftist opposition to impeach or remove the president. Fujimori's victory reinforces Latin America's political shift toward right-wing and center-right governments. She joins leaders including Javier Milei of Argentina, Daniel Noboa of Ecuador, Santiago Peña of Paraguay, Rodrigo Paz of Bolivia, José Raúl Mulino of Panama and José Antonio Kast of Chile. The leaders traveled to Peru to attend Tuesday's inauguration.

results.content:
**Keiko Fujimori has officially been sworn in as Peru’s first female president, marking a historic milestone in a nation that has endured nearly a decade of intense political turbulence and institutional instability.**  
The inauguration ceremony took place in Lima, where Fujimori assumed the highest office in the land, becoming the first woman to lead Peru since the country gained independence. Her ascension to the presidency represents a significant moment not only for gender representation in Latin American politics but also for a country desperately seeking stability after years of governmental chaos.  
Peru has struggled with remarkable political volatility over the past ten years, cycling through multiple presidents and experiencing repeated corruption scandals that have eroded public trust in democratic institutions. The South American nation has witnessed impeachment proceedings, mass protests, and a revolving door of leadership that has hindered economic development and social progress.  
During her inaugural address, Fujimori pledged to address one of Peru’s most pressing challenges by constructing a large-scale prison facility. This commitment comes as the country grapples with overcrowding in its correctional system and rising concerns about public safety. The promise to build a major prison suggests her administration will prioritize law and order issues that have resonated with many Peruvian voters frustrated by crime and insecurity.
The new president’s path to power has been closely watched both domestically and internationally. Her political career has been marked by controversy, given her family’s complex legacy in Peruvian politics. Keiko is the daughter of Alberto Fujimori, who served as Peru’s president from 1990 to 2000 before fleeing the country amid corruption allegations. He was later extradited, tried, and convicted on charges including human rights violations and corruption.  
Despite this complicated family history, Keiko Fujimori has built her own political base over the years. She has campaigned on platforms emphasizing security, economic stability, and infrastructure development. Her supporters view her as a strong leader capable of bringing order to Peru’s chaotic political landscape, while critics remain wary of potential authoritarian tendencies associated with her father’s administration.  
Peru, a country of approximately 33 million people, stands as one of Latin America’s most important economies, rich in natural resources including copper, gold, and silver. However, political instability has hampered investment and economic growth potential. International observers and investors are watching closely to see whether Fujimori’s administration can provide the consistency needed to unlock Peru’s economic potential.
The broader Latin American region has seen increasing female political leadership in recent years, with women serving as presidents in countries including Chile, Honduras, and previously in Argentina and Brazil. Fujimori’s election continues this trend, though her administration faces unique challenges given Peru’s particularly unstable recent political history.  
As President Fujimori begins her term, she inherits a country with deep social divisions, economic inequality, and weakened democratic institutions. Her promise to construct major prison infrastructure signals an initial focus on security concerns, but experts suggest her success will ultimately depend on her ability to foster economic growth, reduce corruption, and restore public confidence in government.  
The international community, particularly neighboring South American nations and key trading partners, will be monitoring Peru’s direction under its first female president as she attempts to navigate the country toward greater stability and prosperity.

results.content:
But in a surprising turn of events, the woman to be sworn in as Peru's new leader on Wednesday was the relatively unknown Dina Boluarte, and not Keiko Fujimori, who had run for the office three times and lost.
There has long been a woman trying - and failing - to become Peru's first female president. But in a surprising turn of events, the woman to be sworn in as Peru's new leader on Wednesday was the relatively unknown Dina Boluarte, and not Keiko Fujimori, who had run for the office three times and lost.
With Congress quickly moving to impeach Mr Castillo, Ms Boluarte was summoned to the building to take the oath of office as president. In her acceptance speech, she called for "a political truce to install a government of national unity". Peru's Congress is notoriously combative and political infighting is the norm. But in a surprise development, one of those who threw her considerable political weight behind Ms Boluarte was Keiko Fujimori, the woman she beat to the presidency.
Her background is very different to that from Ms Fujimori, the daughter of former President Alberto Fujimori, who grew up in the highest political circles in Lima. Ms Boluarte, on the other hand, was born in the southern town of Chalhuanca, the youngest of 14 children. She had first planned to study nursing in Cusco, but decided that she was more interested in law, which she studied in the capital, Lima. For 17 years, she worked for Peru's public records office.
Her political career is short, having run for office for the first time four years ago when she tried to run for the post of mayor of the district of Surquillo in Lima. In 2020, she unsuccessfully ran for Congress for the left-wing Peru Libre party - another thing that sets her apart from Ms Fujimori, who is a right-winger. A year later, she became Mr Castillo's vice-presidential running mate.

results.name: Keiko Fujimori - Wikipedia
results.content:
Fujimori narrowly won the presidency during her fourth attempt in 2026, defeating Roberto Sánchez in the runoff. Fujimori is the second woman to become president of Peru, after Dina Boluarte, and the first to be elected in her own right.
At the 1995 inauguration of Brazilian president Fernando Henrique Cardoso, Fujimori first voiced an ambition to become Peru's first woman president, though she said she was reluctant to enter politics, which she felt had disrupted her family and adolescence. Her parents divorced in 1996.
Fujimori ran for president in four consecutive general elections (2011, 2016, 2021 and 2026) and is the only candidate in modern Peruvian history to reach four consecutive presidential runoffs. She lost the first three by narrow margins before defeating Roberto Sánchez in 2026, becoming the first woman elected president of Peru and returning Fujimorism to power 25 years after her father's government collapsed.

results.name: Keiko Fujimori, President of Peru: A Global Roundup of Reactions
results.content:
Elected after the closest runoff in the country’s recent history — 50.13 per cent to 49.86 per cent, a margin of fewer than 50,000 votes — and sworn in on 28 July 2026, former president Alberto Fujimori’s daughter has prompted the same cluster of reactions from Lima to Asian capitals: doubts about the legitimacy of such a narrow victory, the spectre of democratic backsliding associated with Fujimorismo, the weight of her father’s legacy and a regional realignment towards Washington.  
After three successive defeats in 2011, 2016 and 2021, Keiko Fujimori finally reached Peru’s highest office at the age of 51. Sworn in on 28 July — the national holiday and the thirty-sixth anniversary of her father’s rise to power — the Fuerza Popular leader became the first woman elected to lead the country and the [ninth person to hold the presidency in a decade](https://gestion.pe/peru/peru-vive-su-noveno-cambio-de-presidente-en-diez-anos-con-la-investidura-de-keiko-fujimori-noticia/). Her victory over left-wing rival Roberto Sánchez returns Fujimorismo to power twenty-six years after the fall of Alberto Fujimori, who died in 2024 after serving part of a sentence for corruption and crimes against humanity.
The most alarmed assessment came from [Nueva Sociedad](https://nuso.org/articulo/keiko-fujimori-elecciones-peru/), a journal widely read in Andean academic circles. It argues that Peru had already been governed since 2022 by an authoritarian coalition in which Fujimorismo played a leading role, and that the 2026 election has merely given that coalition electoral legitimacy. Backed by business organisations and armed forces shielded by guarantees of impunity, an unpopular president facing protests in the streets could, judging by her record, resort to repression.
Business circles, by contrast, focused on the promise of stability. Both the [Atlantic Council](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/a-razor-thin-victory-a-divided-nation-what-awaits-perus-next-president/) and [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-28/fujimori-gives-peru-its-best-shot-at-breaking-cycle-of-presidential-chaos) see her arrival as Peru’s best chance to break its chronic cycle of presidential removals. On the geopolitical front, [Reuters](https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2026-07-28/perus-fujimori-takes-power-extending-latin-americas-rightward-tilt) noted her stated interest in closer cooperation with the Trump administration and the “Shield of the Americas,” while [The Washington Times](https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2026/jul/28/keiko-fujimori-inaugurated-perus-president-narrow-election-victory/) detailed a security agenda inspired by El Salvador: a mega-prison modelled on Cecot and judges appearing with their faces concealed.
